The cumulative grazing capacity to be foregone over the life of the operation is expected to be about 5,250 cow-calf units, with additional losses due to land occupied by facilities for the life of the operation. This would amount to about 1,440 acres at the projected level of development, or 48 animal units annually including the 39 mile railroad spur. At the high level, facilities would occupy about 1,800 acres, displacing a grazing capacity of 60 animal units annually.
After mining has progressed through an area, rehabilitation can begin. Eventually, the grazing capacity can be reinstated to some degree. The degree is dependent on the relative successes of reclamation planning, the rehabilitation program, and the range management practices that follow. The efficiency of these processes cannot be fully predicted at this time. There is no long term experience for planned reclamation on surface mined lands in this region. There is, however, sufficient experience with the establishment of seeded grasses on disturbed range land and highway fills to indicate that reclamation may be feasible. However, the magnitude of site disruption caused by surface mining is vastly greater, and success cannot be guaranteed.
It should also be noted that livestock reservoirs and fences will be destroyed. These will have to be replaced before grazing can be effectively implemented and range management practices utilized.
